beats.intro: Chapter eleven. [[sub]]Valuation looks forward, so forecasts matter. This chapter covers what to forecast, how to forecast it, and how to handle uncertainty.
beats.objects: First, what to forecast. There are four kinds of forecast objects. [[drv]]Drivers of financial statement lines, such as stores open and sales per store. Drivers explain growth and often improve accuracy. [[line]]Individual lines, for items without clear drivers or that matter little, such as amortization. [[sum]]Summary measures, such as free cash flow or earnings per share. Efficient, but less transparent. [[adhoc]]And ad hoc objects, such as a legal settlement or a natural disaster, that are not yet in the statements. [[note]]Prefer objects that companies disclose regularly.
beats.approaches: For any object, there are four approaches. [[hist]]Historical results: assume the past repeats. Easy, and reasonable when conditions are stable, but weak for cyclical companies. [[base]]Historical base rates and convergence: assume results drift toward an industry or peer norm. [[mgmt]]Management guidance: useful for company-specific items, but managers may be optimistic, and they have no edge on macro variables. [[disc]]Analyst discretion: your own view of the drivers, best when conditions are changing, such as a cyclical company. [[note]]In practice, analysts combine approaches.
beats.convergence: Convergence is a base-rate idea. [[start]]A company earns a twenty eight percent margin, while its industry earns fifteen. [[curve]]High returns attract competitors, so the gap tends to shrink. If it closes twenty percent each year, the margin falls to twenty five, twenty three, twenty two, twenty, and nineteen percent. [[note]]Forecasting that fade is more realistic than assuming the margin stays at twenty eight forever. The pace of convergence depends on barriers to entry and pricing power.
beats.revenue: Revenue can be forecast from two directions. [[td]]Top-down: the market is ten thousand, growing four percent, to ten thousand four hundred. A twelve percent share gives twelve forty eight. [[bu]]Bottom-up: one hundred twenty stores, each selling ten point four, also gives twelve forty eight. [[gap]]When the two disagree, one has a hidden assumption. Maybe the share is too high, or the stores are too productive. Cross-checking uncovers implicit assumptions. [[note]]Keep non-recurring revenue, such as currency effects, separate from recurring revenue.
beats.workingcap: Costs and working capital follow revenue. [[opex]]Forecast operating expenses so they are coherent with revenue. Cost of sales as a percentage of sales, and fixed costs separately. [[ar]]Receivables come from days sales outstanding. Thirty days on revenue of thirty six fifty is three hundred. [[inv]]Inventory comes from days of inventory. Sixty days on cost of sales of twenty one ninety is three sixty. [[ap]]Payables come from days payable. Forty five days is two seventy. [[nwc]]Net working capital is three hundred, plus three sixty, minus two seventy: three ninety. If sales grow, working capital grows with them, and absorbs cash.
beats.capex: Capital spending has two parts. [[maint]]Maintenance capital spending keeps the existing business running, and is often close to depreciation and amortization. Here, one hundred. [[growth]]Growth capital spending funds expansion, and follows the company's strategy and revenue growth. Here, eighty. [[total]]Total capital spending is one eighty. [[fund]]Where does the money come from? Operating cash flow of one fifty, and thirty of new borrowing. [[note]]Capital structure forecasts start from historical leverage and the company's financial strategy, then adjust for how capital spending is funded.
beats.scenarios: Because the future is uncertain, build scenarios. [[base]]Base case: earnings per share of two dollars, with probability fifty percent. [[bull]]Upside: two sixty, probability twenty five percent. [[bear]]Downside: one twenty, probability twenty five percent. [[ev]]The probability-weighted value is one ninety five. [[note]]The spread between scenarios tells you how much confidence the forecast deserves, and which assumptions matter most.
beats.wrap: Four things to keep. [[w1]]Forecast objects that are regularly disclosed, preferably drivers. [[w2]]Choose among historical results, base rates, guidance and discretion, and combine them. [[w3]]Cross-check top-down and bottom-up revenue, then derive expenses, working capital and capital spending from it. [[w4]]Use scenarios, with probabilities, to show the range of outcomes.
